title: Harpyiae. Buthrotum
titleEn: The Harpies and the Voyage to Buthrotum — Aeneid III.209–305
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Aeneas, still telling Dido the story of his wanderings, has just left Crete behind, and the storm has driven the Trojans to the Strophades, islands in the Ionian Sea where the Harpies live, the bird-women who once plagued king Phineus. The Trojans find unguarded herds, kill and cook some of the cattle and call on the gods, even Jupiter, to share the meal, but the Harpies swoop down and foul the food; when they come a second time the Trojans are waiting with swords, though the birds' feathers turn every blow aside. Celaeno, one of the Harpies and a prophetess, perches on a high rock and accuses them of carrying war to the innocent; she announces on Apollo's authority that they will reach Italy but will not wall their city before hunger drives them to gnaw their very tables. The Trojans lose heart, and Anchises prays to the gods to avert the threat and spare the pious. They sail on past the islands of Ulysses' kingdom, Zacynthos, Dulichium, Same, Neritos and Ithaca, whose land they curse as the nurse of cruel Ulysses, and put in at Actium under the headland of Leucata, where they hold games and Aeneas fixes a captured shield to the doorposts with a verse of dedication. After a winter they sail on, past Corfu and along the coast of Epirus to Buthrotum, where they hear an unbelievable rumour: Helenus, a son of Priam, is king in Greek cities and has married Andromache. Aeneas goes ashore, burning to speak with him, and comes upon Andromache herself in a grove, pouring offerings to the ashes of Hector at an empty tomb.
part: The Harpies and the Voyage to Buthrotum (III.209–305)

sentences.t:
Servatum ex undis Strophadum me litora primum
accipiunt;
sentences.l:
Me, saved from the waves, the shores of the Strophades
first receive;
sentences.i: Rescued from the waves, I am first taken in by the shores of the Strophades;
sentences.n: The part opens on a new paragraph, with Aeneas still the narrator. 'Servatum… me' is the perfect passive participle, 'saved', agreeing with 'me', the object of 'accipiunt': 'the shores receive me, saved from the waves'. 'ex undis' is 'out of the waves', and 'primum' is 'first', the first land reached after the storm. 'Strophadum' is a Greek genitive plural of the Strophades; the next clause tells what they are. 'Servatum' and 'me' are singular because Aeneas, though the whole fleet is saved, tells of his own landing. The Latin Library reads 'excipiunt' for Greenough's 'accipiunt', a difference of nuance only.

sentences.t:
Strophades Graio stant nomine dictae,
insulae Ionio in magno, quas dira Celaeno
Harpyiaeque colunt aliae, Phineia postquam
clausa domus, mensasque metu liquere priores.
sentences.l:
The Strophades stand called by a Greek name,
islands in the great Ionian sea, which dread Celaeno
and the other Harpies inhabit, since Phineus's
house was shut to them, and through fear they left their earlier tables.
sentences.i: The Strophades, which bear a Greek name, are islands in the broad Ionian sea; terrible Celaeno and the other Harpies live there, ever since Phineus's house was closed against them and in terror they abandoned the tables they had before.
sentences.n: 'Strophades… dictae' — 'called the Strophades' 'Graio nomine' is the ablative of the name by which they are called, 'by a Greek name'. 'stant' here is 'stand', 'are'. 'Ionio in magno' is 'in the great Ionian (sea)', with 'mari' understood; the preposition is set between the two adjectives (you'll see this placing constantly). 'quas… colunt' — 'which… inhabit', with two subjects, 'dira Celaeno' and 'Harpyiae aliae'. The Harpies are winged bird-women; in the story told of the Argonauts, they tormented the blind Thracian king Phineus by fouling or snatching his food until the sons of Boreas drove them off, which is the allusion in 'Phineia… domus'. 'postquam clausa (est) domus' — 'since the house was closed', with 'est' understood, 'clausa' being the perfect passive participle. 'liquere' is the old short perfect form for 'liquerunt' (-ere = -erunt, you'll see this constantly), 'they left', 'metu' is an ablative of cause, 'through fear', and 'priores' is 'former, previous'.

sentences.t:
Tristius haud illis monstrum, nec saevior ulla
pestis et ira deum Stygiis sese extulit undis.
sentences.l:
No monster is more grim than they, nor has any
plague or wrath of the gods more savage lifted itself from Stygian waves.
sentences.i: No monster is more dismal than these, and no plague or wrath of the gods more savage ever came up out of the Stygian flood.
sentences.n: 'Tristius haud illis monstrum' — 'no monster is grimmer than they' ('tristius' is a comparative; 'haud' negatives it; 'illis' is an ablative of comparison, 'than they', with no 'quam'). 'nec saevior ulla pestis' — 'nor any more savage plague'; 'pestis' is feminine, hence 'ulla'. 'ira deum' — 'the wrath of gods'; 'deum' is the old genitive plural (-um for -orum, you'll see this constantly). 'sese extulit' — 'raised itself out', 'sese' being the emphatic form of 'se'. The Styx is the river of the underworld, so 'Stygiis undis' sets their origin in the world below. The next line, with no verb, goes on to describe them.

sentences.t:
Virginei volucrum voltus, foedissima ventris
proluvies, uncaeque manus, et pallida semper
ora fame.
sentences.l:
Maiden faces of the birds, the filthiest discharge
of the belly, and hooked hands, and faces ever pale
with hunger.
sentences.i: They have the faces of maidens upon the bodies of birds; a most foul flux comes from their bellies; their hands are hooked, and their faces are always wan with hunger.
sentences.n: A new sentence with no verb describes the Harpies: a list of nouns, with 'have' or 'are' understood. 'Virginei volucrum voltus' — 'the faces of maidens, the faces of the birds' ('volucrum' is a genitive plural of the noun 'volucris', 'bird'; 'voltus' is Greenough's spelling of 'vultus'). 'foedissima… proluvies' — 'the foulest outflow', 'proluvies' being a nominative singular in -es; 'ventris' is 'of the belly'. 'uncae manus' — 'hooked hands', that is, claws. 'pallida… ora' — 'pale faces' (note 'ora' is the plural of 'os, oris', 'face', 'mouth'), and 'fame' is an ablative of cause, 'with hunger'. Line 218, 'ora fame', is a half-line: Greenough prints it short, one of the places where Virgil left a verse unfinished. The Latin Library prints 'uultus', the same word.

sentences.t:
Huc ubi delati portus intravimus, ecce
laeta boum passim campis armenta videmus,
caprigenumque pecus nullo custode per herbas.
sentences.l:
Hither when borne we entered the harbours, behold,
glad herds of cattle we see all over the fields,
and a goat-born flock with no keeper through the grass.
sentences.i: As soon as we had been carried here and sailed into the harbours, we saw, to our delight, herds of cattle scattered over the fields and a flock of goats with no one to watch them on the grass.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Huc ubi delati portus intravimus' — 'when carried here we entered the harbours'; 'delati' is the perfect passive participle of 'defero', nominative plural agreeing with the 'we' of 'intravimus'. 'portus' here is accusative plural. 'ecce' is 'behold'; it is a vivid pointing word. 'laeta… armenta' — 'glad herds', and 'laetus' said of cattle also means 'thriving, fat', and the herds are fine ones. 'caprigenum pecus' — 'the goat-born flock': 'caprigenum' is an adjective (accusative neuter singular) agreeing with 'pecus', and the phrase stands for 'goats'. 'nullo custode' is an ablative absolute with no participle, 'no keeper (being there)'.

sentences.t:
Inruimus ferro, et divos ipsumque vocamus
in partem praedamque Iovem;
sentences.l:
We rush on them with the sword, and the gods and Jove himself we call
to a share and to the plunder;
sentences.i: We fell on them with our swords and called on the gods, and on Jupiter himself, to come and share in the spoil;
sentences.n: 'Inruimus ferro' — 'we rush on (them) with the iron', 'ferro' being the ablative of means, 'by sword'; it is the plain poetic word for the blade. 'divos' is the accusative plural of 'divus', 'god', the poetic word beside 'deus'. 'in partem praedamque' — 'to a share and to the booty', a loose pair: they invite the gods in to share what they take. 'ipsumque… Iovem' puts Jupiter, the king of gods, among those invited. The sentence continues in the next unit.

sentences.t:
tum litore curvo
exstruimusque toros, dapibusque epulamur opimis.
sentences.l:
then on the curved shore
we both build couches and feast on rich fare.
sentences.i: and then on the curving shore we set out couches and feasted on a bountiful meal.
sentences.n: 'tum litore curvo' — 'then on the curved shore'; 'litore' is the ablative of place with no preposition (you'll see this constantly in poetry). 'exstruimusque toros' — 'we build up couches' (the 'toros' are the couches on which the banqueters reclined); 'exstruimusque… dapibusque' is the double '-que… -que', 'both… and'. 'epulamur' is a deponent verb (passive in form, active in sense): 'we feast'. 'dapibusque… opimis' — 'with rich feasts', the ablative of means.

sentences.t:
At subitae horrifico lapsu de montibus adsunt
Harpyiae, et magnis quatiunt clangoribus alas,
diripiuntque dapes, contactuque omnia foedant
immundo;
sentences.l:
But suddenly with a horrifying swoop from the mountains the Harpies
are upon us, and with great clangs they beat their wings,
and they snatch the feasts, and everything they befoul
with unclean touch;
sentences.i: But suddenly, with a terrible swoop from the hills, the Harpies were on us, beating their wings with a great clatter; they tore away the food and fouled it all with their filthy touch;
sentences.n: 'At subitae… adsunt Harpyiae' — 'suddenly the Harpies are present'; 'subitae' is an adjective with the force of an adverb, a Latin habit ('subitae' agrees with 'Harpyiae'). 'horrifico lapsu' — 'with a terrifying swoop', ablative of manner. 'magnis… clangoribus' — 'with great clangings', ablative of means, with 'quatiunt alas', 'they shake their wings'. 'diripiuntque dapes' — 'and they tear the feasts to pieces', that is, snatch. 'contactuque… immundo' — 'by an unclean touch', ablative of means, 'contactus' being a fourth-declension noun; 'omnia foedant' — 'defile everything'. The narration is in the historic present ('adsunt', 'quatiunt'), as at 219–224: a Latin way of making a scene vivid.

sentences.t: tum vox taetrum dira inter odorem.
sentences.l: then a dread cry amid a foul stench.
sentences.i: and amid the foul stench came a dreadful cry.
sentences.n: A verbless clause, 'tum (est) vox dira inter taetrum odorem' — 'then (there is) a dread voice amid a foul smell'. The order is interlaced: 'taetrum', the adjective of 'odorem', stands first and 'dira', the adjective of 'vox', follows it, so 'inter' lands between the two phrases (hyperbaton). 'dira' comes again at 235, 256 and 262.

sentences.t:
Rursum in secessu longo sub rupe cavata,
arboribus clausi circum atque horrentibus umbris,
instruimus mensas arisque reponimus ignem:
sentences.l:
Again in a deep retreat, beneath a hollowed rock,
shut in all around by trees and by bristling shades,
we set out the tables and put back fire on the altars:
sentences.i: Again, in a deep recess under a hollowed rock, closed in on every side by trees and by shadows that bristle with branches, we set out the tables and lay a fire anew on the altars.
sentences.n: 'Rursum in secessu longo' — 'again in a long retreat'; the 'secessus' is a secluded recess (a cove or hollow). 'sub rupe cavata' — 'under a hollowed rock'. 'arboribus clausi circum atque horrentibus umbris' — 'closed all round by trees and bristling shadows'; 'clausi' is the perfect passive participle, nominative plural, with ablative of means; 'circum' here is an adverb, 'round about'. 'horrentibus' means 'bristling, shaggy', and the shadows bristle with branches. 'arisque reponimus ignem' — 'and we put the fire back on the altars' (the prefix 're-' means 'again' or 'back': they redo the sacrifice); 'aris' (dative or ablative) is 'on the altars'. The colon introduces the second attack.

sentences.t:
rursum ex diverso caeli caecisque latebris
turba sonans praedam pedibus circumvolat uncis,
polluit ore dapes.
sentences.l:
again from the opposite quarter of the sky and from blind hiding-places
a noisy crowd flies round the plunder on hooked feet,
and pollutes the feast with its mouth.
sentences.i: Again, from a different quarter of the sky, out of hidden lairs, the clamouring flock wheels about the spoil on its hooked claws and fouls the food with its mouths.
sentences.n: 'rursum ex diverso caeli' — 'again from the opposite part of the sky' ('ex diverso' means 'from the opposite direction'; 'caeli' is the genitive, 'of the sky'). 'caecisque latebris' — 'and blind hiding places', where 'caecus' means 'unseen, hidden', not 'blind'. 'turba sonans' — 'the crowd, sounding, noisy'. 'praedam pedibus circumvolat uncis' — 'flies round the plunder with hooked feet' (ablative of means; 'circumvolat' takes an accusative). 'ore' is the ablative of means, 'with the mouth', the singular put for the plural of all their mouths. The sentence ends partway through the line, at the stop after 'dapes'.

sentences.t:
Sociis tunc, arma capessant,
edico, et dira bellum cum gente gerendum.
sentences.l:
To my comrades then I proclaim: let them take up arms,
and that war must be waged with the dread race.
sentences.i: Then I give my men an order: they are to take up their weapons, and we must make war on this horrible tribe.
sentences.n: 'Sociis… edico' — 'to my comrades I proclaim, I order' ('edico' with a dative). 'arma capessant' is a command in the subjunctive without 'ut' (an indirect command, 'that they take up arms'; 'capesso' is a frequentative of 'capio'). 'et dira bellum cum gente gerendum' — 'and that war must be waged with the dread race', completing the order with 'esse' understood: 'bellum gerendum (esse)', an accusative and infinitive with the gerundive of obligation (you'll see this constantly). 'dira' is parted from 'gente' by 'bellum cum' (hyperbaton).

sentences.t:
Haud secus ac iussi faciunt, tectosque per herbam
disponunt enses et scuta latentia condunt.
sentences.l:
No otherwise than ordered they do, and the swords
they set hidden here and there through the grass, and they conceal the shields that lie unseen.
sentences.i: They do exactly as they are told: they place their swords here and there, hidden in the grass, and they stow away their shields out of sight.
sentences.n: 'Haud secus ac iussi faciunt' — 'not otherwise than ordered they do', 'iussi' being the perfect passive participle of 'iubeo', 'having been ordered'; 'haud secus ac' means 'just as, no differently from'. 'tectos… enses' — 'hidden swords' ('tectos' in agreement with 'enses'), 'per herbam', 'through the grass'. 'disponunt' means 'they arrange in separate places'. 'scuta latentia condunt' — 'they hide the shields that lie hidden', 'latentia' being the neuter plural of the present participle 'latens', 'lying hidden'. The Latin Library has 'ensis', the accusative plural spelled with -is; the sense is the same.

sentences.t:
Ergo ubi delapsae sonitum per curva dedere
litora, dat signum specula Misenus ab alta
aere cavo.
sentences.l:
Then when, swooping down, they gave their noise along the curved
shores, from a high lookout Misenus gives the signal
with hollow bronze.
sentences.i: Then, when the Harpies swept down and made their din along the winding shore, Misenus gave the signal from a high watch-post with his hollow bronze.
sentences.n: 'Ergo ubi delapsae sonitum per curva dedere litora' — 'so when, having glided down, they gave their sound along the curving shores'; 'delapsae' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'delabor', feminine plural (the Harpies); 'dedere' is the old perfect 'dederunt' (-ere = -erunt, you'll see this constantly). 'dat signum… Misenus' — Misenus is the Trojan trumpeter, who will die and be buried at Cumae in Book 6. 'specula… ab alta' — 'from a high lookout'; 'specula' is a watch-post. 'aere cavo' — 'with hollow bronze', ablative of means, 'aes' being the common poetic word for a bronze trumpet. Greenough's sentence stops after 'cavo.' in the middle of line 240.

sentences.t:
Invadunt socii, et nova proelia temptant,
obscenas pelagi ferro foedare volucres:
sentences.l:
Our comrades charge, and try a strange sort of battle,
to defile the filthy birds of the sea with the sword:
sentences.i: Our men rush in and try an unheard-of kind of fight, to wound the foul birds of the sea with steel;
sentences.n: 'Invadunt socii' — 'the comrades attack'. 'nova proelia temptant' — 'they try new battles', 'new' in the sense of strange, since the enemy is a bird. 'obscenas pelagi… volucres' — 'the foul birds of the sea'; 'obscenas' means 'foul, ill-omened' and 'pelagi' is the genitive of 'pelagus', 'the sea', a Greek word (neuter, in -us). 'foedare' is the infinitive 'to defile, mutilate', a poetic infinitive explaining 'proelia temptant', 'they try the battle to…'. The colon introduces the result in the next line.

sentences.t:
sed neque vim plumis ullam nec volnera tergo
accipiunt, celerique fuga sub sidera lapsae
semesam praedam et vestigia foeda relinquunt.
sentences.l:
but neither force on their feathers nor wounds on their backs
they take, and in swift flight, up under the stars, gliding,
they leave their half-eaten prey and foul traces.
sentences.i: But they take no blow on their plumage and no wound in their backs; in swift flight they glide up beneath the stars and leave behind their half-eaten spoil and their foul traces.
sentences.n: 'sed neque vim plumis ullam nec volnera tergo accipiunt' — 'but they receive neither any force on their feathers nor wounds on their back'; 'volnera' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulnera'. The Harpies are supernatural, and weapons cannot hurt them. 'celerique fuga sub sidera lapsae' — 'gliding in swift flight under (up to) the stars'; 'lapsae' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'labor', feminine plural, and 'sub' with the accusative means 'up to, towards'. 'semesam praedam' — 'the half-eaten prey' ('semesus' is the participle of 'semiedo'), and 'vestigia foeda' are the foul marks they leave behind.

sentences.t:
Una in praecelsa consedit rupe Celaeno,
infelix vates, rumpitque hanc pectore vocem:
sentences.l:
One on a very high rock sat down, Celaeno,
ill-omened prophetess, and breaks this speech from her breast:
sentences.i: One of them perched on a towering crag, Celaeno, a prophetess of ill luck, and out of her breast she burst this utterance:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Una… Celaeno' — 'one, Celaeno'; 'Una', the first word, picks out a single Harpy, and the name is placed last. 'praecelsa' means 'very high'. 'consedit' is the perfect of 'consido', 'sat, perched'. 'infelix vates' — 'ill-fated, ill-omened prophetess'; 'vates' is the usual word for an inspired seer and is here feminine. 'rumpit… vocem' — 'she breaks (forth) a voice', a poetic phrase for starting to speak. The colon opens her speech, which Greenough prints with a mark of quotation.

sentences.t:
“Bellum etiam pro caede boum stratisque iuvencis,
Laomedontiadae, bellumne inferre paratis,
et patrio Harpyias insontis pellere regno?
sentences.l:
“War even for the slaughter of oxen and bullocks laid low,
sons of Laomedon, war too do you make ready to bring,
and to drive the guiltless Harpies from their father's kingdom?
sentences.i: “Is it war, then, in return for slain oxen and bullocks struck down, descendants of Laomedon, is it war that you are preparing to bring, and to drive the innocent Harpies out of their ancestral realm?
sentences.n: Celaeno's speech opens (the mark “ is Greenough's). 'Bellum etiam' — 'war too', 'etiam' marking it as an extra insult on top of the slaughter. 'pro caede boum stratisque iuvencis' — 'in return for the killing of oxen and the bullocks laid low'; 'pro' with the ablative, here 'for, in exchange for'. 'Laomedontiadae' is a vocative, 'sons of Laomedon': Laomedon, the king of Troy, cheated gods of their pay and broke his word, and the title taunts the Trojans with the faith-breaking of their ancestor. 'bellumne inferre paratis' — 'do you prepare to bring war?', with '-ne' marking a question, repeating 'bellum' for emphasis. 'patrio… regno' — ablative of separation, 'from the ancestral kingdom'. 'insontis' is an accusative plural in -is. 'Harpyias' is the Greek accusative plural.

sentences.t:
Accipite ergo animis atque haec mea figite dicta,
quae Phoebo pater omnipotens, mihi Phoebus Apollo
praedixit, vobis Furiarum ego maxuma pando.
sentences.l:
Take it, then, in your minds, and fix these words of mine,
which the almighty Father to Phoebus, Phoebus Apollo to me
foretold; to you I, greatest of the Furies, lay them open.
sentences.i: Take it to heart, then, and fix these words of mine in your minds: the prophecy the almighty Father gave to Phoebus, and Phoebus Apollo to me, I, foremost of the Furies, now unfold before you.
sentences.n: 'Accipite ergo animis atque haec mea figite dicta' — two imperatives, 'accept' and 'fix'; 'animis' is the ablative of place, 'in your minds', and 'dicta' is 'sayings, words'. 'quae Phoebo pater omnipotens, mihi Phoebus Apollo praedixit' — the relative 'quae' is the object of 'praedixit', 'foretold', and a single verb serves two subjects, 'pater omnipotens' (Jupiter) and 'Phoebus Apollo', with two datives, 'Phoebo' and 'mihi': the prophecy passes from Jupiter to Apollo to Celaeno. 'Furiarum ego maxuma' — 'I, the greatest of the Furies' ('Furiarum' is a partitive genitive; 'maxuma' is Greenough's spelling); Celaeno claims the rank of a Fury here, avengers of crime. 'pando' means 'I lay open, reveal'.

sentences.t:
Italiam cursu petitis, ventisque vocatis
ibitis Italiam, portusque intrare licebit;
sentences.l:
For Italy you aim by your course, and with the winds called
you will go to Italy, and to enter its harbours will be allowed;
sentences.i: You are bound for Italy, and with the winds you have called on you shall go to Italy and be allowed to enter its harbours;
sentences.n: 'Italiam cursu petitis' — 'you seek Italy by your course', the present tense with the force of 'you are on your way to'. 'ventisque vocatis' is an ablative absolute, 'the winds having been called', that is, summoned by prayer. 'ibitis Italiam' — 'you will go to Italy', the future of 'eo'; the accusative of the goal is used without a preposition with a country's name, as with a town (a poetic use). 'portusque intrare licebit' — 'and it will be permitted (to you) to enter harbours', 'licebit' being the impersonal verb with an infinitive as its subject. The semicolon prepares the contrast with 'sed'.

sentences.t:
sed non ante datam cingetis moenibus urbem,
quam vos dira fames nostraeque iniuria caedis
ambesas subigat malis absumere mensas.”
sentences.l:
but not before you gird the granted city with walls,
than dread hunger and the wrong of our slaughter
drive you to eat up the tables gnawed round with your jaws.”
sentences.i: but you shall not ring with walls the city granted to you until terrible hunger, and the wrong done in killing our cattle, force you in your jaws to gnaw your very tables and eat them away.”
sentences.n: 'sed non ante datam cingetis moenibus urbem quam…' — 'but not before you gird the given city with walls than…', 'ante… quam' set apart, 'quam' only coming in the next line. 'datam urbem' — the city granted by fate. The verb after 'quam' is the subjunctive 'subigat', which expresses something awaited or intended, 'before hunger shall drive you'. 'dira fames' — 'dread hunger'. 'nostraeque iniuria caedis' — 'and the wrong of our slaughter', the 'nostrae' being the Harpies' own, referring to the killing of their cattle. 'subigat… absumere' — 'drive (you) to eat up'. 'ambesas… mensas' — 'tables eaten round'; 'malis' is the ablative of means, 'with jaws' ('mala' is the jaw). This curse comes true in Book 7, where the Trojans eat the flat loaves they have set their food on. The closing mark ” belongs to the end of the speech.

sentences.t: Dixit, et in silvam pennis ablata refugit.
sentences.l: She spoke, and, borne off on her wings, fled back into the forest.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and on her wings she was carried off and fled back into the wood.
sentences.n: 'Dixit' is the tag that ends a speech (you'll see this constantly). 'pennis ablata' — 'carried off on her wings', 'ablata' being the perfect passive participle of 'aufero', feminine, with 'pennis' in the ablative of means. 'refugit' — 'fled back' (the prefix 're-' marks the return to where she came from).

sentences.t:
At sociis subita gelidus formidine sanguis
deriguit;
sentences.l:
But to my comrades with sudden fear the cold blood
stiffened;
sentences.i: But the blood of my comrades went cold and stiff with sudden terror;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'At sociis… gelidus… sanguis deriguit' — 'but to my comrades the cold blood stiffened'; 'sociis' is a dative of the person affected, 'for/to the comrades', and 'subita… formidine' is an ablative of cause, 'with sudden fear'. 'deriguit' is the perfect of 'derigesco', 'it stiffened'.

sentences.t:
cecidere animi, nec iam amplius armis,
sed votis precibusque iubent exposcere pacem,
sive deae, seu sint dirae obscenaeque volucres.
sentences.l:
their spirits fell, and no longer with arms,
but with vows and prayers they bid peace be asked for,
whether they be goddesses or dread and foul birds.
sentences.i: their courage failed, and they urge that peace be sought, no longer by weapons but by promises and prayers, whether these creatures be goddesses or terrible and filthy birds.
sentences.n: 'cecidere animi' — 'the spirits fell'; 'cecidere' is the old form of 'ceciderunt' (-ere = -erunt, you'll see this constantly). 'nec iam amplius armis, sed votis precibusque' — 'no longer with arms, but with vows and prayers' (ablatives of means). 'iubent exposcere pacem' — 'they bid (someone) demand peace': the comrades are the subject, the person bidden is left unexpressed (in the next lines it is Anchises who prays), and 'exposcere' is the infinitive 'to ask earnestly'. 'sive deae, seu sint dirae obscenaeque volucres' — 'whether (they are) goddesses or are dread and foul birds'; 'deae' is the nominative plural, 'sint' is understood with 'deae' from the second clause, its subjunctive being that of an indirect alternative ('whether they are… or…'), and 'sive… seu' is simply 'whether… or'. The sailors do not know what the Harpies are.

sentences.t:
Et pater Anchises passis de litore palmis
numina magna vocat, meritosque indicit honores:
sentences.l:
And father Anchises, with palms spread out from the shore,
calls the great powers, and proclaims the honours deserved:
sentences.i: And father Anchises, holding out his palms from the shore, called on the great divinities and appointed the offerings due to them:
sentences.n: 'passis de litore palmis' — 'with palms spread out, from the shore' ('passis' is the perfect participle of 'pando', 'spread', not of 'patior'; 'palmis' means 'palms of the hands', the usual gesture of prayer to heaven). 'numina magna' — 'the great powers'; a 'numen' is a divine will or presence. 'meritosque indicit honores' — 'and proclaims the due honours', the rites and offerings the gods have earned; 'meritos' is the participle of the deponent 'mereor' with passive sense, 'deserved'. The colon introduces his prayer, whose opening mark “ stands at 265.

sentences.t:
“Di, prohibete minas; di, talem avertite casum,
et placidi servate pios!
sentences.l:
“Gods, ward off these threats; gods, turn aside such a mishap,
and kindly save the pious!”
sentences.i: “Gods, keep these threats away; gods, avert so dire a mischance, and in your kindness spare those who do their duty!”
sentences.n: The prayer opens with the mark “. 'Di' is the contracted plural of 'deus' (here a vocative, 'O gods'), repeated for solemnity. 'prohibete minas' — 'keep off the threats'; 'talem avertite casum' — 'turn away such a mishap'. 'placidi servate pios' — 'kindly (placidi, nominative plural agreeing with the gods) save the pious'; 'pios' is the accusative plural used as a noun, 'those who are dutiful', a word the poem uses of Aeneas himself and of his people. In Greenough's text the closing mark is printed after a space and with no space before the next word ('pios! ”Tum'), so a cut after the mark would fall in the middle of a word: this unit stops at 'pios!', the closing mark is carried in `l` and `i` here, and in the edition it stands at the head of the next unit's `t`.

sentences.t:
”Tum litore funem
deripere, excussosque iubet laxare rudentes.
sentences.l:
Then from the shore to tear off the cable, and to loosen
the ropes shaken out, he bids.
sentences.i: Then he orders us to cast the cable off from the shore, and to let the shaken-out ropes run slack.
sentences.n: The edition prints the closing mark of Anchises's prayer glued to 'Tum', so it stands at the head of this unit's `t`. 'Tum… iubet' — 'then he orders'; the subject is Anchises, the object (us) is understood, and the two infinitives 'deripere' and 'laxare' depend on 'iubet'. 'litore funem deripere' — 'to tear the cable from the shore', 'litore' being the ablative of separation, 'funem' the mooring cable. 'excussosque… rudentes' — 'and the ropes shaken out'; 'excussos' is the perfect passive participle, 'rudentes' the ropes of the rigging (accusative plural). The Latin Library prints 'rudentis' for the same case.

sentences.t: Tendunt vela Noti;
sentences.l: The south winds stretch the sails;
sentences.i: The south winds fill and stretch the sails;
sentences.n: 'Tendunt vela Noti' — 'the Souths stretch the sails'. 'Noti' is the nominative plural of 'Notus', the south wind, and here the winds as a force. 'tendunt' means 'stretch taut'.

sentences.t:
fugimus spumantibus undis,
qua cursum ventusque gubernatorque vocabat.
sentences.l:
we flee over foaming waves,
where both wind and helmsman were calling our course.
sentences.i: and we flee over the foaming waters, wherever the wind and the helmsman called our course.
sentences.n: 'fugimus spumantibus undis' — 'we flee on the foaming waves' (ablative of the route). 'qua' is 'where, by which way'. 'cursum ventusque gubernatorque vocabat' — 'both wind and helmsman were calling (the) course'; the singular verb 'vocabat' agrees with the nearer of two subjects, and 'vocare cursum' is 'to summon a course', to point the way. The double '-que… -que' ties the two subjects together.

sentences.t:
Iam medio adparet fluctu nemorosa Zacynthos
Dulichiumque Sameque et Neritos ardua saxis.
sentences.l:
Now in the middle of the swell wooded Zacynthos appears,
and Dulichium, and Same, and Neritos steep with crags.
sentences.i: Now, in the midst of the swell, wooded Zacynthos comes into view, with Dulichium, Same and Neritos, towering with its rocks.
sentences.n: 'Iam medio adparet fluctu' — 'now in the middle of the swell appears' ('adparet' is Greenough's spelling of 'apparet', and 'medio fluctu' an ablative of place). Zacynthos, Dulichium, Same and Neritos are islands off the west coast of Greece in the kingdom of Ulysses, as Homer names them in the Odyssey. 'nemorosa' means 'wooded'. 'Dulichiumque Sameque et Neritos' — the '-que… et' joins the three names; 'Same' is a Greek first-declension nominative. 'ardua saxis' — 'steep with rocks', an ablative of respect, 'saxis' being the rocks.

sentences.t:
Effugimus scopulos Ithacae, Laertia regna,
et terram altricem saevi exsecramur Ulixi.
sentences.l:
We escape the rocks of Ithaca, the kingdom of Laertes,
and we curse the land that nursed fierce Ulysses.
sentences.i: We slip past the crags of Ithaca, Laertes' realm, and call down curses on the land that nursed the pitiless Ulysses.
sentences.n: 'Effugimus scopulos Ithacae' — 'we escape the rocks of Ithaca'. 'Laertia regna' is in apposition to 'scopulos Ithacae' as a whole: 'the Laertian realm', the kingdom of Laertes, who was the father of Ulysses. 'terram altricem' — 'the nurse land' ('altricem' is the accusative of 'altrix', a feminine noun used as an adjective, 'nourishing'), the land that bred him. 'saevi exsecramur Ulixi' — 'we curse… of savage Ulixes'; 'Ulixi' is taken here as a genitive (it is a Greek name that Latin sometimes declines on the model of the second declension), 'saevi' agreeing with it. Ulysses is hated as the Greek whose tricks destroyed Troy, which is why the Trojans curse his homeland.

sentences.t:
Mox et Leucatae nimbosa cacumina montis
et formidatus nautis aperitur Apollo.
sentences.l:
Soon the cloudy peaks of Mount Leucata too
and Apollo, feared by sailors, is opened to view.
sentences.i: Next the cloud-covered summits of the Leucatan hill, and Apollo, whom sailors dread, are laid open to sight.
sentences.n: 'Mox et Leucatae nimbosa cacumina montis' — 'soon, too, the cloudy summits of mount Leucata'; 'Leucatae' is the genitive singular of the Greek name Leucate (a headland on the island of Leucas, by Actium), agreeing with 'montis'. 'nimbosa' means 'full of clouds'. 'formidatus nautis… Apollo' — 'Apollo, dreaded by sailors', where 'nautis' is a dative of the agent with the perfect passive participle 'formidatus'. 'aperitur' is 'is opened up, comes into view'. 'Apollo' means his temple on the headland.

sentences.t: Hunc petimus fessi et parvae succedimus urbi;
sentences.l: This we seek, weary, and approach a small town;
sentences.i: We make for it, worn out, and come up to a little town;
sentences.n: 'Hunc' (masculine) looks back to 'Apollo', the god's shrine on the headland, or to the mount; either way it is the headland they make for. 'petimus fessi' — 'we seek it, tired' (the adjective 'fessi' in the nominative plural agrees with 'we', for 'tired as we are'). 'parvae succedimus urbi' — 'we approach the small town'; 'succedo' takes a dative (here 'urbi') when it means 'go up to'.

sentences.t: ancora de prora iacitur, stant litore puppes.
sentences.l: the anchor is thrown from the prow, the sterns stand on the shore.
sentences.i: The anchor is cast from the bows, and the ships stand with their sterns on the beach.
sentences.n: 'ancora de prora iacitur' — 'the anchor is thrown from the prow'; the verb is in the present passive, in the narrative present. 'stant litore puppes' — 'the sterns stand on the shore': 'puppes' (literally 'sterns') stands for 'ships', and 'litore' is again an ablative of place without a preposition.

sentences.t:
Ergo insperata tandem tellure potiti,
lustramurque Iovi votisque incendimus aras,
Actiaque Iliacis celebramus litora ludis.
sentences.l:
So, having possessed at last the land unhoped for,
we purify ourselves to Jove and kindle the altars with offerings,
and we throng the Actian shores with Trojan games.
sentences.i: So, having reached at last a land we had not hoped for, we hold the rite of purification to Jupiter, light the altars with our votive gifts and fill the shores of Actium with games in the Trojan manner.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'insperata tandem tellure potiti' — 'having got possession at last of the unhoped-for land'; 'potiti' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'potior', which takes the ablative ('tellure'). 'lustramurque Iovi' — 'we are purified (we purify ourselves) to Jove', a passive used in a middle sense; 'lustro' means to purify with a ritual, and 'Iovi' is the dative of the god honoured. 'votisque incendimus aras' — 'and with vows we kindle the altars', 'votis' being the offerings promised in prayer. 'Actiaque… litora' — 'the Actian shores'; Actium was to be the site of Octavian's victory in 31 BC, and Virgil's readers would have known it, so the games Aeneas holds there are the poem's early nod to the Augustan Actian games. 'Iliacis… ludis' — 'with Iliac (Trojan) games', ablative of means.

sentences.t:
Exercent patrias oleo labente palaestras
nudati socii;
sentences.l:
My comrades, stripped, practise the wrestling of their fathers
with sliding oil;
sentences.i: My companions strip, and with the oil gliding over their limbs they practise the wrestling that their fathers knew;
sentences.n: 'Exercent patrias oleo labente palaestras' — 'they exercise the ancestral wrestling-schools'; 'palaestras' stands for the exercise itself, and 'patrias' marks it as the Trojans' native sport. 'oleo labente' is an ablative absolute, 'the oil gliding', that is, the oil (rubbed on) running over their bodies. 'nudati socii' — 'the stripped comrades', 'nudati' being the perfect passive participle of 'nudo'.

sentences.t:
iuvat evasisse tot urbes
Argolicas, mediosque fugam tenuisse per hostis.
sentences.l:
it pleases to have got away from so many Argive cities
and to have held our flight through the midst of enemies.
sentences.i: We are glad to have got clear of so many Greek cities and to have held our flight on through the midst of the foe.
sentences.n: 'iuvat evasisse tot urbes Argolicas' — 'it is pleasing to have escaped so many Argive cities'; 'iuvat' is an impersonal verb whose subject is the perfect infinitive 'evasisse', and 'evado' takes an accusative here. 'Argolicas' means 'of Argolis', that is, Greek, as 'Argive' does throughout the poem. 'mediosque fugam tenuisse per hostis' — 'and to have held a flight through the midst of enemies'; 'medios' agrees with 'hostis' (accusative plural in -is), and 'fugam tenuisse' is 'kept up a flight'.

sentences.t:
Interea magnum sol circumvolvitur annum,
et glacialis hiemps aquilonibus asperat undas.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile the sun rolls round the great year,
and icy winter roughens the waves with north winds.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the sun makes its circuit of the great year, and icy winter with its north winds stirs the waves to roughness.
sentences.n: 'Interea magnum sol circumvolvitur annum' — 'meanwhile the sun rolls round the great year'; 'magnum annum' is an accusative of extent, 'through the great year', the whole circuit. 'circumvolvitur' is a passive with the sense 'rolls itself round'. 'glacialis hiemps' — 'icy winter' (Greenough's 'hiemps' is the old spelling of 'hiems'). 'aquilonibus asperat undas' — 'roughens the waves with north winds', 'aquilonibus' an ablative of means. The change of season tells us they have stayed at Actium through the winter.

sentences.t:
Aere cavo clipeum. magni gestamen Abantis,
postibus adversis figo, et rem carmine signo:
sentences.l:
A shield of hollow bronze, the carried weight of great Abas,
I fasten on the facing doorposts, and mark the deed with a verse:
sentences.i: A shield of hollow bronze, once the burden of mighty Abas, I fix to the facing doorposts, and I mark the deed with a verse:
sentences.n: The print has 'clipeum.' with a full stop, a misprint for a comma (the next word, 'magni', is lower-case, and 'magni gestamen Abantis' is in apposition to 'clipeum'). The Latin is kept exactly as Greenough prints it, and the translation reads the comma. 'Aere cavo clipeum' — 'a shield of hollow bronze' ('aere cavo' is an ablative of material); 'gestamen' is 'what is carried'; 'magni Abantis' — 'of great Abas', whose shield it was (the verse that follows says the arms came from the Greeks). 'postibus adversis figo' — 'I fasten to the opposite doorposts'; 'figo' is 'fix'. 'rem carmine signo' — 'I mark the thing with a verse', the dedication given next.

sentences.t: AENEAS HAEC DE DANAIS VICTORIBVS ARMA.
sentences.l: AENEAS THESE FROM DANAANS VICTORIOUS ARMS.
sentences.i: Aeneas set up these arms, taken from the victorious Greeks.
sentences.n: The inscription, in capitals as Greenough prints it (VICTORIBVS with V for U, as on Roman stone). It is a complete hexameter with no verb: 'Aeneas (dedicates, set up) these arms from the victorious Danaans' — 'haec arma' is the object, 'de Danais victoribus' means 'from (taken from) the victorious Greeks', and a verb such as 'dat' or 'dicat' is understood, as is usual on dedications. 'Danais' is the ablative plural of 'Danai', 'the Greeks'.

sentences.t: Linquere tum portus iubeo et considere transtris:
sentences.l: To leave the harbours then I order, and to sit on the benches:
sentences.i: Then I order my men to quit the harbours and take their seats at the rowing-benches:
sentences.n: 'Linquere tum portus iubeo et considere transtris' — 'to leave the harbours then I order, and to sit down on the benches'; the object of 'iubeo' (the comrades) is understood, and the two infinitives 'linquere' and 'considere' depend on it. 'portus' is an accusative plural. 'transtris' is the ablative of place with no preposition (the benches, 'transtra', are the rowers' seats across the ship).

sentences.t: certatim socii feriunt mare et aequora verrunt.
sentences.l: in rivalry my comrades strike the sea and sweep the levels.
sentences.i: The crew strike the sea in rivalry, each trying to outdo the next, and sweep the flat water with their oars.
sentences.n: 'certatim' is an adverb, 'in a contest, vying'. 'feriunt mare' — 'strike the sea' (with oars). 'aequora verrunt' — 'sweep the levels', 'aequora' being the plain surface of the sea, 'verrunt' being 'sweep, brush', a rowing word used of oars.

sentences.t:
Protinus aërias Phaeacum abscondimus arces,
litoraque Epiri legimus portuque subimus
Chaonio, et celsam Buthroti accedimus urbem.
sentences.l:
Straightway we hide the lofty citadels of the Phaeacians,
and we skirt the coasts of Epirus and enter the
Chaonian harbour and approach the high city of Buthrotum.
sentences.i: Without a pause we drop the high towers of the Phaeacians out of sight behind us; we coast along the shores of Epirus, steer into the Chaonian harbour and come up to the lofty city of Buthrotum.
sentences.n: 'Protinus aërias Phaeacum abscondimus arces' — 'straight on we hide the airy towers of the Phaeacians'; 'abscondimus' is a nautical way of saying that the land sinks out of sight behind the ship. 'aërias' (Greenough prints the diaeresis) means 'high in the air'; 'Phaeacum' is the genitive plural of 'Phaeaces' (a plural of the third declension, whose genitive ends in -um): the Phaeacians are the Homeric sailors of Scheria (identified with Corfu), who took Ulysses home. 'litoraque Epiri legimus' — 'we skim the shores of Epirus' (a Latin sailor's phrase: 'lego' is 'gather up, pass close by'). 'portuque subimus Chaonio' — 'and we approach (enter) the Chaonian harbour', 'Chaonius' being an adjective for the district of Epirus. 'celsam Buthroti accedimus urbem' — 'and we draw near the high city of Buthrotum' ('Buthroti' is the genitive of the Greek name).

sentences.t:
Hic incredibilis rerum fama occupat auris,
Priamiden Helenum Graias regnare per urbes,
coniugio Aeacidae Pyrrhi sceptrisque potitum,
et patrio Andromachen iterum cessisse marito.
sentences.l:
Here an unbelievable rumour of events seizes our ears,
that Helenus, Priam's son, rules over Greek cities,
having won the marriage and the sceptres of Pyrrhus, descendant of Aeacus,
and that Andromache has passed again to a husband of her own land.
sentences.i: Here an incredible report of happenings fills our ears: Priam's son Helenus is king in Greek cities, having taken over the marriage and the sceptre of Pyrrhus, a descendant of Aeacus, and Andromache has passed a second time to a husband of her own people.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'incredibilis rerum fama' — 'an unbelievable rumour of things'; 'auris' is an accusative plural in -is. The rumour is given in an accusative and infinitive (the content of 'fama'): 'Priamiden Helenum… regnare' — 'that Helenus, Priam's son, rules' ('Priamiden' is a Greek patronymic, accusative). Helenus is a Trojan prophet-prince, a son of Priam. 'Graias… urbes' — 'Greek cities'. 'coniugio Aeacidae Pyrrhi sceptrisque potitum' — 'having got the marriage and sceptres of Pyrrhus the Aeacid'; 'potitum' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'potior', governing the ablatives, and 'Aeacidae' is the Greek genitive of 'Aeacides', a descendant of Aeacus (Pyrrhus is the son of Achilles, grandson of Peleus, great-grandson of Aeacus). 'et patrio Andromachen iterum cessisse marito' — 'and that Andromache had gone again to a husband of her own country'; 'Andromachen' is a Greek accusative, 'cessisse' a perfect infinitive, 'patrio… marito' a dative, 'a husband from her fatherland', and 'iterum' means that she has remarried: Pyrrhus carried her off from Troy, and now she belongs to another Trojan. The Latin Library has 'urbis' for Greenough's 'urbes', a case-ending variant that changes nothing.

sentences.t:
Obstipui, miroque incensum pectus amore,
compellare virum et casus cognoscere tantos.
sentences.l:
I was struck dumb, and my heart was set on fire with wondrous
desire to address the man and learn of such great fortunes.
sentences.i: I stood stunned, and a wondering eagerness kindled my heart to speak with the man and hear of such great fortunes.
sentences.n: 'Obstipui' — 'I was stupefied'. 'miroque incensum pectus amore' — 'and my heart kindled with a wondrous longing', where 'incensum' is the perfect passive participle with 'est' understood, and 'miro amore' is an ablative of cause. The two infinitives 'compellare' ('to address') and 'cognoscere' ('to learn') explain the longing (you'll see this constantly: the infinitive after a noun of desire). 'virum' is the man, Helenus. 'casus… tantos' — 'such great fortunes, happenings'.

sentences.t:
Progredior portu, classis et litora linquens,
sollemnis cum forte dapes et tristia dona
ante urbem in luco falsi Simoentis ad undam
libabat cineri Andromache,
sentences.l:
I go forward from the harbour, leaving the fleet and the shore,
when by chance the solemn feasts and the sad gifts
before the city, in a grove, by the wave of a false Simois,
was pouring to the ashes Andromache,
sentences.i: I walked on from the harbour, leaving my fleet and the shore behind, and just then, by chance, before the city, in a grove, beside the water of a counterfeit Simois, Andromache was pouring out the yearly feast and the doleful gifts to the ashes of the dead,
sentences.n: 'Progredior portu' — 'I go forward from the harbour' ('portu' is an ablative of separation). 'classis et litora linquens' — 'leaving the fleet and the shore', 'linquens' being the present participle and 'classis' an accusative in -is. 'sollemnis cum forte dapes et tristia dona… libabat… Andromache' — a 'cum' clause with the indicative where the sense is 'when just then'; 'sollemnis' is the accusative plural in -is, 'solemn, yearly' (the funeral meal at fixed times), and 'libabat' is the imperfect of 'libo', 'was pouring out as an offering'. The word order puts the objects first and the subject last, keeping the reader waiting for the name. 'cineri' is a dative, 'to the ashes'. 'falsi Simoentis' — 'of a false Simois': 'falsi' means that this is only a copy, a stream given the name of the river at Troy; 'Simoentis' is the genitive of a Greek name.

sentences.t:
Manisque vocabat
Hectoreum ad tumulum, viridi quem caespite inanem
et geminas, causam lacrimis, sacraverat aras.
sentences.l:
and she called the Shades to Hector's tomb, which empty
with green turf, and the twin altars, a cause for tears,
she had consecrated.
sentences.i: and she was calling the Shades to Hector's mound, an empty tomb of green turf which she had hallowed, with two altars besides, a cause of her tears.
sentences.n: 'Manisque vocabat' — 'and she called the Manes' (the spirits of the dead; 'Manis' is an accusative plural in -is). 'Hectoreum ad tumulum' — 'to the tomb of Hector' ('Hectoreus' is the adjective), with 'ad' placed between adjective and noun. 'viridi quem caespite inanem et geminas… sacraverat aras' — 'which, empty, with green turf, and the twin altars she had consecrated'; 'quem' is the relative, the object of 'sacraverat' (pluperfect) with 'geminas… aras' ('twin altars') as a second object; 'inanem' means 'empty': it is a cenotaph, since Hector's body lay in Troy, so the tomb holds no remains. 'causam lacrimis' — 'a cause for tears', an apposition to the whole thing she had set up, with 'lacrimis' in the dative.
